prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as my single-part, two-name position, and the first round has sharpened rather than weakened it. The decisive step is conceptual and I can judge it from my own field: Katori's magic-wavelength condition, where the differential polarisability of the clock states vanishes, lets many neutral atoms be held in a lattice with Doppler and recoil shifts suppressed and the clock transition left unperturbed. That is what turned a 10^-15 single-ion-style measurement into a many-atom 10^-18 one, and it is a different object from the comb or from single-ion control. Ye's group then carried the strontium lattice clock to record accuracy and stability, including control of collisional and spin-exchange shifts. The result is mature in the sense I weigh most: Sr, Yb and Hg lattice clocks agree across independent laboratories, are intercompared internationally, and already give millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements and bounds on drifting constants. The two names map onto two identifiable contributions, concept and record realisation, so the three-person limit does not force an arbitrary cut. I would defend this on the statute's discovery-or-invention criterion and not on opening support counts.
statement.case_against: The serious objection, which I have not removed, is novelty relative to the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize: a colleague can fairly say the lattice clock is a refinement of honoured tools and a precision advance, not a new phenomenon. Credit at the margin also remains open, since Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, and ion-clock groups reaching 10^-18, have close claims that two names cannot capture. Finally, the SI second has not yet been redefined, and Ye's involvement in the thorium nuclear clock is a neighbouring storyline the citation must not absorb. If the committee judges the overlap with 2005 and 2012 to be decisive, I accept that this prize would be harder to justify than I have argued.

responses.point: Olsson would leave Ye's many-body and spin-exchange clock work out of the citation as a second storyline that dilutes a clean one, and says the redefinition of the second is a consequence of the result, not its justification.
responses.response: I accept the substance of your point and have changed my drafting. In round 1 I wanted Ye's many-body control inside the citation. I now think it belongs in the case but not in the wording: spin-exchange and collisional control are part of what made 10^-18 reachable, so they are covered by the phrase 'bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level' without a separate clause. A second named storyline would invite exactly the lattice-versus-ion adjudication we want to avoid. I also agree on the redefinition: it follows from the result, and our timing should not follow the metrology community's calendar.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers magic-angle graphene as a new phenomenon nobody expected from carbon, treats the clocks as a refinement of a lineage honoured in 2005 and 2001, and says he would not oppose a precision-measurement prize.
responses.response: Your distinction between a new phenomenon and a refinement is the real disagreement, and I do not think it is settled by counting. The frequency comb is the readout ruler and laser cooling is a tool; neither contains the idea that a lattice can be tuned so the trapping itself does not shift the clock line. That is an invention with consequences in physics, not only in engineering. I share your admiration for B022 and keep it as my first alternative. But as long as the pairing mechanism and the correlated states remain open and the experimental credit leaves out Cao, I would be uneasy writing a citation that has to say what the discovery means. I am glad you would not oppose B036, because that is the question on which the vote may turn.

responses.point: Mehlig moved to B022 after reading the ballots, argues that the prize rests on flat-band-driven correlated phases and not on a theory of superconductivity, and accepts B036 as a strong fallback if B022 is judged premature.
responses.response: Your framing, that the citation honours the prediction and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states and not a mechanism, is the strongest answer to my maturity worry, and I have weighed it. Two difficulties remain for me. The discovery claim names superconductivity, so the open mechanism is visible in the citation itself, and the credit is not repaired: Cao is the first author of the decisive papers, and Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto preceded Bistritzer and MacDonald on moire bands. On the clock side I grant your overlap point but think it is smaller than you do, for the reason I gave Danielsson. If the committee wants a younger field-opening prize, I do not think this is the year; a settled interpretation of the superconductivity would change my view.

responses.point: Eriksson said he would take B036 seriously if Kroll and Lindroth could show the magic-wavelength idea is the decisive conceptual step, and notes that he moved B036 from eighth to a second alternative.
responses.response: I take that as the right test, so here is the argument stated directly. Before the lattice proposal, neutral-atom clocks faced a trade-off between atom number, which gives statistics, and the motional and light-shift systematics that confinement introduces. At the magic wavelength the AC Stark shifts of the two clock levels cancel to first order, and deep Lamb-Dicke confinement removes first-order Doppler and recoil effects. The remaining limits are then higher-order polarisabilities, blackbody and collisions, each of which can be measured, and that is why 10^-18 became an engineering-and-physics programme and not a hope. This is atomic-structure physics of the kind I calculate, and I think it is the decisive step. I also agree that your own candidate has the weaker credit position because of the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang gap.

responses.point: Kroll proposes the same two names, would give the citation a lattice-and-10^-18 framing, and has disclosed a possible recusal question from his stay in the Hall laboratory, whose JILA lineage is linked to Ye's group.
responses.response: We agree on the configuration; two points of caution. First, I would resist the framing of the pending redefinition as part of our case, since Olsson and Pearce are right that the result stands without it. Second, on recusal, as I read your note the tie is a doctoral research stay in a laboratory that is part of the same institutional lineage, with no documented link to Katori or Ye. That is a close call and the committee should decide it openly, but I would not myself treat it as disqualifying. If you abstained, the position would still have my support and, by the chair's summary, that of at least three others, so I do not think the choice turns on your vote.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues accept the lattice clock as a distinct invention separate from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which is a judgement and not a factual matter.

Whether the credit among Katori, Ye, Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto and the national-laboratory groups can be drawn narrowly enough that the citation does not look arbitrary; I rely on my own knowledge of the early lattice-clock history and have not verified priority details independently.
Whether the committee would take B022 if the interpretation of the correlated states settles further, and what new evidence would shift the choice this year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. For transparency, my long-running collaboration with Anne L'Huillier, colleagues in the Lund attosecond group, and Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich concerns attosecond photoionisation and does not involve the lattice-clock candidates. I have no documented tie to the credited names of the other shortlisted candidates, and my disclosure is unchanged since round 1.
